investigations.title: Burning and Suppression of Solids
investigations.principal_investigator: Dr. Paul V. Ferkul (NCSER / NASA GRC)
investigations.summary: Investigated the burning characteristics and extinction limits of solid spherical and flat fuel samples in microgravity under quiescent and low forced convective flow conditions (0.5 to 5.0 cm/s). Evaluated gaseous extinguishment by inert gas flow cessation and nitrogen dilution.

investigations.title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II
investigations.principal_investigator: Dr. Sandra L. Olson (NASA Glenn Research Center)
investigations.summary: Expanded on BASS by examining flame stabilization and blow-off extinction limits of solid slab fuels over extended oxygen concentrations (14% to 25%) and diverse flow velocities to benchmark numerical flame models.

investigations.title: Spacecraft Fire Experiment - I
investigations.principal_investigator: Dr. David L. Urban (NASA Glenn Research Center)
investigations.summary: First large-scale spacecraft fire test in history conducted inside the pressurized module of an uncrewed Cygnus cargo craft. Tested a 0.4m x 1.0m cotton-fiberglass composite fabric sample under low-velocity forced flow.

runs.ignition_method: Continuous linear hot-wire at intake end

investigations.title: Spacecraft Fire Experiment - II
investigations.principal_investigator: Dr. David L. Urban (NASA Glenn Research Center)
investigations.summary: Assessed material flammability limits across nine discrete samples (acrylic, Nomex, silicone, SIBAL) in microgravity to evaluate NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 terrestrial screening predictions against actual spaceflight behavior.

investigations.title: Spacecraft Fire Experiment - III
investigations.principal_investigator: Dr. David L. Urban (NASA Glenn Research Center)
investigations.summary: Re-examined large-scale flame spread on 0.4m x 1.0m fabric under elevated forced air velocity (25 cm/s) to quantify aerodynamic flame propagation enhancement and downstream toxic soot generation.

investigations.title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment
investigations.principal_investigator: Dr. David L. Urban (NASA Glenn Research Center)
investigations.summary: Characterized the particle size distribution of smoke produced in microgravity by overheating typical spacecraft materials. Established that microgravity smoke contains far larger agglomerated particulates than Earth smoke due to lack of buoyancy-driven dilution.

investigations.title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment - Reflight
investigations.principal_investigator: Dr. David L. Urban (NASA Glenn Research Center)
investigations.summary: Reflight investigation with higher-resolution mobility spectrometers and condensation particle counters to measure real-time agglomeration dynamics of overheated silicone, Nomex, and printed circuit board substrates.

investigations.title: Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test
investigations.summary: Evaluated the operational efficacy of commercial optical particle sizers and condensation particle counters in microgravity aboard ISS to define future spacecraft smoke detector calibration standards.

investigations.title: Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test - 2
investigations.principal_investigator: Dr. Marit Meyer (NASA Glenn Research Center)
investigations.summary: Investigated airborne particulate behavior, cabin air recirculation filtration efficiency, and optical obscuration profiles for submicron and supermicron particulate fractions.

investigations.title: Flame Extinguishment Experiment
investigations.principal_investigator: Dr. Forman A. Williams (UC San Diego) / Dr. Vedha Nayagam
investigations.summary: Landmark droplet combustion investigation that revealed the existence of low-temperature quasi-steady 'cool flames' in hydrocarbon combustion following apparent radiative extinction in microgravity.

runs.suppression_agent: CO2 gas dilution (radiative cool flame transition)

investigations.title: Flame Extinguishment Experiment - 2
investigations.principal_investigator: Dr. Forman A. Williams (UC San Diego)
investigations.summary: Expanded droplet combustion to binary fuel mixtures (heptane/hexadecane) and varied diluent gases (CO2, N2, He) to study soot formation suppression and second-stage cool flame extinction thresholds.

investigations.title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments
investigations.principal_investigator: Dr. Peter B. Sunderland (Univ. of Maryland) et al.
investigations.summary: Suite of five standalone gaseous burner investigations (CFI, B-FIRE, s-Flame, E-FIELD, CLEEN) examining spherical diffusion flames, electric field flame steering, soot inception, and dilution extinction limits.

investigations.title: Solid Fuel Ignition and Extinction
investigations.principal_investigator: Dr. James S. T'ien (Case Western Reserve Univ.) / Dr. Paul Ferkul
investigations.summary: Modular test facility on ISS measuring ignition delay, flame growth rate, and extinction boundaries for thick composite materials under Exploration Atmospheres (56.5 kPa, 34% O2) and low convective flow regimes.

research_gaps.gap_title: Absence of Partial-Gravity (0.16g Moon & 0.38g Mars) Flammability Benchmarks
missing_parameters: Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI) under weak buoyant convection
Critical radiant heat flux for thick polymers in partial-g
research_gaps.physical_explanation: In 0g (microgravity), transport is governed purely by molecular diffusion and forced ventilation. In 1g (Earth), strong buoyant upward flow sweeps away heat while drawing fresh oxygen to the flame base. In partial gravity (0.16g Lunar and 0.38g Martian), buoyant velocity U_buoyant ~ sqrt(g * L * delta_T / T_inf) is sluggish: fast enough to supply fresh oxidizer to the flame front, but too slow to cool the reaction zone by thermal blow-off. This creates a dangerous 'partial-gravity peak hazard zone' where flame spread rates and material flammability can actually exceed both 0g and 1g limits.
research_gaps.recommended_experiments: Deploy centrifugally spun combustion chambers aboard ISS (or Artemis lunar surface combustion testbeds) to systematically vary gravity from 0.05g to 0.5g under Exploration Atmosphere conditions (56.5 kPa / 34% O2).

research_gaps.gap_title: Exploration Atmosphere (56.5 kPa / 34% O2) Flammability Envelope Mismatch
research_gaps.missing_regime: Hypobaric Hyperoxic Exploration Atmosphere (56.5 kPa, 34% O2)
missing_parameters: Auto-ignition temperature of composite electronics wiring at 56.5 kPa
Extinction velocity thresholds at sub-atmospheric pressure
Soot yield index at 34% O2 in low convective velocity
research_gaps.physical_explanation: NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 flammability acceptance ratings were historically performed at terrestrial 101.3 kPa with upward flame propagation. Reduced cabin pressure (56.5 kPa) increases molecular diffusion coefficients (D ~ 1/P), while elevated oxygen (34%) steepens reaction rates. Terrestrial 1g test data cannot reliably predict whether materials rated self-extinguishing on Earth will support catastrophic sustained burning in an Artemis habitat.
research_gaps.recommended_experiments: Conduct systematic SoFIE runs across varied polymers at 56.5 kPa and 34% O2 across forced flow rates between 1 cm/s and 25 cm/s.

research_gaps.gap_title: Microgravity Smoke Particle Coagulation & Optical Sensor Calibration Blindspot
missing_parameters: In-situ agglomeration rate constant for silicone and Kapton pyrolysis
Optical scattering cross-section of large microgravity soot clusters (>2.0 um)
Alarm threshold delay time under habitat ventilation velocities (<10 cm/s)
research_gaps.physical_explanation: Data from SAME and SAME-R demonstrated that microgravity smoke particles coagulate into large agglomerates (mean diameter 1.5 - 3.0 um) compared to Earth 1g smoke (0.05 - 0.3 um) because of the absence of buoyant dilution and prolonged residence times in the hot reaction zone. Terrestrial ionization detectors fail to register these large particles, while standard optical scatter detectors may experience substantial signal lag or false alarms in low-velocity recirculation loops.
research_gaps.recommended_experiments: Calibrate multi-wavelength laser scattering and condensation particle counters in long-duration microgravity to establish flight certification standards for Artemis Gateway and lunar lander smoke alarm suites.

research_gaps.gap_title: Cool Flame Suppression Dynamics with Inactive Diluent Gases
research_gaps.missing_regime: Low-Temperature Chemical Kinetics in Microgravity Quenching
missing_parameters: Low-temperature chemical kinetic rate constants for alkane droplet extinction
Radiative loss fraction during cool flame regime
Secondary re-ignition hazards upon post-fire cabin re-pressurization
research_gaps.physical_explanation: FLEX and FLEX-2 experiments proved that hydrocarbon fuels can continue burning in an invisible, low-temperature (~400-600°C) cool flame mode after primary visible flame extinction when suppressed with CO2 or N2. If astronauts assume a fire is fully extinguished and restore ventilation or oxygen flow, secondary explosive thermal runaway can occur.
research_gaps.recommended_experiments: Investigate cool flame extinction limits for liquid propellants and hydraulic fluids under varying partial pressure of inert extinguishants in the Combustion Integrated Rack.

document_chunks.section_title: Large-Scale Flammability on Cygnus Resupply Vehicle
document_chunks.citation_str: Urban, D.L., et al., 'Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire-I) Final Report,' NASA/TM-2017-219582, pp. 4-12, 2017.
document_chunks.chunk_text: The Saffire-I flight test demonstrated that a 0.4 m wide by 1.0 m long cotton-fiberglass blend (SIBAL) fabric burned vigorously in microgravity under an airflow velocity of 20 cm/s at 20.9% oxygen and 100.5 kPa. The steady-state flame spread rate was measured at 1.85 mm/s. Unlike terrestrial tests where buoyant upward flow causes flame flickering and turbulent detachment, the microgravity flame exhibited a remarkably stable, uniform parabolic luminous zone with flame extinction observed only upon vehicle atmospheric dump.

document_chunks.section_title: Solid Sample Extinction and Quiescent Limits
document_chunks.citation_str: Ferkul, P.V. & Olson, S.L., 'Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS) Operational Results,' NASA/TM-2014-218386, 2014.
document_chunks.chunk_text: In the Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS) experiment in the Microgravity Science Glovebox, cast PMMA rods and flat SIBAL sheets were subjected to low forced flow velocities from 0.5 to 5.0 cm/s in air. For PMMA rods (12.7 mm diameter) at 21% O2 and 101.3 kPa, the flame spread rate was 0.08 mm/s at 1.2 cm/s flow. As forced flow was reduced below 0.5 cm/s, radiative heat loss from the flame to the surrounding chamber exceeded convective chemical heat release, causing radiative extinction without needing chemical suppressants.

document_chunks.section_title: Discovery of Microgravity Droplet Cool Flames
document_chunks.citation_str: Nayagam, V., Dietrich, D.L., Ferkul, P.V., & Williams, F.A., 'Can cool flames support quasi-steady alkane droplet burning?,' Nature Communications, 4:2688, 2013.
document_chunks.chunk_text: During Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) testing in the Combustion Integrated Rack aboard the ISS, n-heptane droplets (initial diameter 2.5 mm) burning in air at 101.3 kPa exhibited apparent flame extinction due to radiative cooling. However, droplet diameter measurements revealed continued burning at temperatures of 600-800 K with zero visible soot or visible emission. This confirmed quasi-steady cool-flame combustion supported by low-temperature chemistry, representing a critical safety consideration for spacecraft liquid fuel leaks.

document_chunks.section_title: Smoke Particle Agglomeration Dynamics in Spacecraft
document_chunks.citation_str: Urban, D.L., Ruff, G.A., & Mulholland, G.W., 'Particle Size Distribution from Overheated Spacecraft Materials,' SAE Technical Paper 2008-01-2053, 2008.
document_chunks.chunk_text: The Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME) on ISS evaluated smoke particles generated from pyrolyzing Teflon wire insulation and Kapton film under microgravity conditions. Particle size measurements demonstrated a shift toward supermicron agglomerates, with volume-mean diameters exceeding 1.5 to 2.5 micrometers, compared to sub-0.1 micrometer diameters on Earth. The absence of buoyancy extends the residence time in the high-temperature zone, promoting rapid Brownian and shear-induced coagulation.

document_chunks.citation_str: T'ien, J.S., Ferkul, P.V., & Johnston, M., 'Solid Fuel Ignition and Extinction (SoFIE) Science Requirements,' NASA/TP-2022-000412, 2022.
document_chunks.chunk_text: The SoFIE investigation examines thick PMMA slabs and composite textiles under NASA Exploration Atmosphere conditions (56.5 kPa total pressure, 34% O2 concentration). Because total pressure is reduced from sea level 101.3 kPa, molecular diffusion is accelerated, while 34% oxygen sustains high adiabatic flame temperatures. Experimental runs with 25 mm PMMA cylinders at 10 cm/s flow showed flame spread rates of 0.38 mm/s, demonstrating that low-velocity cabin drafts in hypobaric exploration modules can maintain intense combustion.
